title: Jeter-Pillars: smooth sound, show music for a white club
summary: Jeter and Pillars stressed tone and quality; in a segregated nightclub they played show tunes with little soloing.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: because they had a different style of band. They wanted to play something -- not like a Guy Lombardo, not like -- but they stressed quality in their band because they were very good musicians.
Where did they get those names from? Were they Mexicans or something?

No, Pillar -- they were black. Jeeter was very light. He was very light. His name was James Jeeter. And the tenor play was named Hays Pillars. And they had a fellow named Charles Pillars. Both of them played in the band. But they stressed -- not like the Benny Moten style, not like Hot Lips was playing or not like McKinney's Cotton Pickers. We had a job in a club so consequently, we had to play a lot of --

-- shows and there wasn't too much room for playing solos in there most of the time. Because after the show, you'd have to play something like -- some of the stocks, you know. That was what the people wanted to hear, you know.

Yes, dancing. And it was a white club, blacks weren't allowed in there. Just for the shows, you know. And we had a special door we had to come in and all that. It was the same old thing. Same old South, like the South. And that was primarily where I was raised, in the nightclub. After I left the Morrison Grenadiers, the bands around Columbus, Ohio,

joined Jester-Pillars, we had to play like (humming). "Doing the Continental" and all the tunes from "Stormy Weather," all the tunes from the shows. That's what we played. So to play that, you had to play with more quality, you know, Tone. They stressed that.
